L0: # scMRDR: A scalable and flexible framework for unpaired single-cell multi-omics data integration
L1: 
L2: Jianle Sun, Chaoqi Liang, Ran Wei, Peng Zheng, LEI BAI, Wanli Ouyang, Hongliang Yan, Peng Ye
L3: 
L4: 【0†Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 38 Main Conference (NeurIPS 2025)】 Main Conference Track
L5: 
L6: 【1†Bibtex】 【2†Paper】
L7: ## Abstract
L8: Advances in single-cell sequencing have enabled high-resolution profiling of diverse molecular modalities, while integrating unpaired multi-omics single-cell data remains challenging. Existing approaches either rely on pair information or prior correspondences, or require computing a global pairwise coupling matrix, limiting their scalability and flexibility.
L9: In this paper, we introduce a scalable and flexible generative framework called single-cell Multi-omics Regularized Disentangled Representations (scMRDR) for unpaired multi-omics integration.
L10: Specifically, we disentangle each cell’s latent representations into modality-shared and modality-specific components using a well-designed $\beta$-VAE architecture, which are augmented with isometric regularization to preserve intra-omics biological heterogeneity, adversarial objective to encourage cross-modal alignment, and masked reconstruction loss strategy to address the issue of missing features across modalities.
L11: Our method achieves excellent performance on benchmark datasets in terms of batch correction, modality alignment, and biological signal preservation. Crucially, it scales effectively to large-scale datasets and supports integration of more than two omics, offering a powerful and flexible solution for large-scale multi-omics data integration and downstream biological discovery.

L5: # Stage 2: Model training【1†】
L6: In this tutorial, we will show how to train a GLUE model to integrate unpaired single-cell multi-omics data. We continue with the previous example of scRNA-seq and scATAC-seq data integration.
L7: 
L8:     [1]:
L9: 
L10: 
L11:     from itertools import chain
L12: 
L13:     import anndata as ad
L14:     import itertools
L15:     import networkx as nx
L16:     import pandas as pd
L17:     import scanpy as sc
L18:     import scglue
L19:     import seaborn as sns
L20:     from matplotlib import rcParams
L21: 
L22: 
L23:     [2]:
L24:     scglue.plot.set_publication_params()
L25:     rcParams["figure.figsize"] = (4, 4)
L26: ## Read preprocessed data【2†】
L27: 
L28: First, read the preprocessed data as produced by 【3†stage 1】.
L29: 
L30:     [3]:
L31: 
L32: 
L33:     rna = ad.read_h5ad("rna-pp.h5ad")
L34:     atac = ad.read_h5ad("atac-pp.h5ad")
L35:     guidance = nx.read_graphml("guidance.graphml.gz")
L36: ## Configure data【4†】
L37: 
L38: > (Estimated time: negligible)
L39: 
L40: Before model training, we need to configure the datasets using 【5†scglue.models.configure_dataset】. For each dataset to be integrated, we need to specify a probabilistic generative model. Here we model the raw counts of both scRNA-seq and scATAC-seq using the negative binomial distribution (`"NB"`).
L41: Optionally, we can specify whether only the highly variable features should be used (`use_highly_variable`), what data layer to use (`use_layer`), as well as what preprocessing embedding (`use_rep`) to use as first encoder transformation.
L42: 
L43:   * For the scRNA-seq data, we use the 【6†previously backed up】 raw counts in the “counts” layer, and use the PCA embedding as the first encoder transformation.
L44:   * For the scATAC-seq data, the raw counts are just `atac.X`, so it’s unnecessary to specify `use_layer`. We use the LSI embedding as the first encoder transformation.
L45: 
L46:     [4]:
L47: 
L48: 
L49:     scglue.models.configure_dataset(
L50:         rna, "NB", use_highly_variable=True,
L51:         use_layer="counts", use_rep="X_pca"
L52:     )
L53: 
L54: 
L55:     [5]:
L56: 
L57: 
L58:     scglue.models.configure_dataset(
L59:         atac, "NB", use_highly_variable=True,
L60:         use_rep="X_lsi"
L61:     )
L62: Other useful options of 【5†scglue.models.configure_dataset】 include:
L63: 
L64:   * `use_batch`: Setting this to an `obs` column tells the model to treat it as a batch effect to be corrected for;
L65: 
L66:   * `use_cell_type`: Setting this to an `obs` column tells the model to use it as cell type supervision.
L67: Next, as we are only using highly-variable features, we also extract a subgraph containing only these highly variable features from the full guidance graph:
L68: 
L69:     [6]:
L70: 
L71: 
L72:     guidance_hvf = guidance.subgraph(chain(
L73:         rna.var.query("highly_variable").index,
L74:         atac.var.query("highly_variable").index
L75:     )).copy()
L76: ## Train GLUE model【7†】
L77: 
L78: > (Estimated time: 15-60 min, depending on computation device)
L79: 
L80: Next we train a 【8†GLUE model】 for integrating the two omics layers.
L81: 
L82:   * The datasets to be integrated are specified as a `dict`, where the keys are domain names. The domain names can be set at your discretion, as long as they are kept consistent (see below).
L83: 
L84:   * Here we specified a directory to the fit function where model snapshots and training logs will be stored.
L85:   * For more advanced usages, please refer to the 【9†function documentation】.
L86: 
L87:     [7]:
L88: 
L89: 
L90:     glue = scglue.models.fit_SCGLUE(
L91:         {"rna": rna, "atac": atac}, guidance_hvf,
L92:         fit_kws={"directory": "glue"}
L93:     )
